learner_notice: Commit one response before feedback appears. Entry checks are low stakes, and a missed fresh re-entry returns control without exit credit.

items.title: Starting check: identify the mobilized fuel
items.prompt: During fasting, adipose triacylglycerol is hydrolyzed. Which product is released for transport to oxidative tissues?
options: Glycogen particles packaged inside lipoproteins
Fatty acids carried through blood with albumin
Ketone bodies stored inside adipose droplets
Glucose covalently attached to serum proteins
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Guided practice: place mitochondrial entry
items.prompt: A long-chain fatty acid has entered a muscle cell and has been activated. Which step is needed before beta oxidation in the mitochondrial matrix?
options: Conversion of the fatty acid into glycogen
Export of acetyl-CoA into the bloodstream
Use the carnitine shuttle for matrix entry
Synthesis of a peptide carrier by ribosomes
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Less help: identify oxidation products
items.prompt: Which set of products most directly results from repeated beta-oxidation cycles?
options: Acetyl-CoA, NADH, and FADH2
Glucose, ATP, and molecular nitrogen
Glycogen, carbon dioxide, and urea
Lactate, ribose, and peptide bonds
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: On your own: connect cis unsaturation to packing
items.prompt: Compared with a saturated fatty acid of similar length, what does a cis double bond most directly do?
options: Straightens the chain and raises packing efficiency
Removes every carbon from the hydrocarbon chain
Converts the fatty acid into a peptide
Introduces a bend that reduces tight packing
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Near exit: trace fasting fatty-acid flow
items.prompt: During an overnight fast, which sequence best traces a fatty acid from adipose storage to oxidation in muscle?
options: Adipose glycogen release → chylomicron transport → nuclear oxidation
Lipolysis → albumin transport → uptake → beta oxidation
Ketone storage → insulin release → cytosolic glycogen synthesis
Protein translation → bile packaging → lysosomal glycolysis
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Changed exit: predict hepatic ketone production
items.prompt: A prolonged fast increases hepatic fatty-acid oxidation while carbohydrate availability remains low. Which change is most consistent?
options: The liver converts every fatty acid directly into glycogen
Adipose tissue stops releasing fatty acids immediately
More acetyl-CoA enters ketone synthesis and export
Long-chain acyl groups bypass mitochondria and become proteins
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: restore the transport sequence
items.prompt: Which carrier–fuel pairing is correct during adipose fatty-acid mobilization?
options: Albumin carries nonesterified fatty acids in blood
Hemoglobin carries triacylglycerol inside red cells
DNA carries acetyl-CoA between organs
Glycogen carries ketone bodies through lymph
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: trace a new tissue destination
items.prompt: Adipose tissue releases fatty acids during fasting. Which path delivers a long-chain fatty acyl group to liver beta oxidation?
options: Albumin transport → liver uptake → glycogen packaging → nuclear entry
Lipoprotein storage → ribosomal activation → cytosolic fermentation
Ketone uptake → adipose synthesis → bile secretion
Albumin → liver uptake → activation → carnitine shuttle
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: connect acetyl-CoA to ketone export
items.prompt: Which condition most directly favors hepatic ketone-body production?
options: Low fatty-acid oxidation with abundant carbohydrate oxidation
High fat oxidation with sustained low carbohydrate
Complete absence of acetyl-CoA in liver mitochondria
Immediate conversion of every amino acid into glycogen
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: apply the state to a new case
items.prompt: A liver cell shows high beta-oxidation flux and rising mitochondrial acetyl-CoA during prolonged fasting. What exported fuel is expected to increase?
options: Glycogen particles released into plasma
Long-chain proteins secreted as fuel
Ketone bodies delivered to extrahepatic tissues
DNA fragments used for muscle oxidation
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Starting check: classify storage synthesis
items.prompt: A liver links many glucose units into glycogen after a meal. How should this process be classified?
options: Catabolic oxidation that removes every glucose carbon
Protein translation directed by messenger RNA
Anabolic polysaccharide storage through glycogenesis
Beta oxidation of fatty acyl chains
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Guided practice: choose a fed-state storage route
items.prompt: A cell has abundant carbon, ATP, and reducing power after immediate needs are met. Which process stores energy in a reduced carbon form?
options: Fatty-acid and triacylglycerol synthesis
Beta oxidation followed by ketone consumption
Glycogen breakdown followed by glucose release
Proteolysis followed by amino-acid oxidation
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Less help: identify nontemplate synthesis
items.prompt: Why is glycogen synthesis called nontemplate synthesis?
options: Because glycogen forms without enzymes or regulation
Because glycogen contains no covalent bonds
Because glucose units are copied from a DNA sequence
No nucleic-acid template specifies glucose-unit order
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: On your own: distinguish build from breakdown
items.prompt: Which pairing correctly matches an anabolic process with its storage product?
options: Beta oxidation → acetyl-CoA release
Glycogenesis → glycogen storage
Lipolysis → circulating fatty acids
Proteolysis → free amino acids
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Near exit: predict fed-state storage
items.prompt: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, insulin action is high and immediate ATP demand is met. Which pair of net processes is most consistent?
options: Adipose lipolysis and hepatic ketone export
Muscle proteolysis and amino-acid oxidation
Glycogen synthesis and triacylglycerol storage
Glycogen breakdown and fatty-acid mobilization
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Changed exit: distinguish template use
items.prompt: A diagram compares protein synthesis, glycogen synthesis, and fatty-acid synthesis. Which statement correctly separates them?
options: All three copy monomer order directly from messenger RNA
Only glycogen synthesis uses a DNA sequence template
Fatty-acid synthesis is translation at a membrane ribosome
Protein is template-directed; glycogen and fatty acids are not
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: use the build-or-break test
items.prompt: Which feature identifies an anabolic storage process?
options: Energy assembles smaller units into stored molecules
A stored molecule is hydrolyzed to release circulating fuel
Reduced carriers transfer electrons to oxygen
A carbon chain is shortened into acetyl-CoA units
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: classify a new storage case
items.prompt: A muscle cell uses glucose units to extend a branched glycogen molecule after exercise recovery. Which description fits?
options: Catabolic glycolysis that consumes glycogen
Anabolic glycogenesis restores carbohydrate storage
Fatty-acid oxidation that generates ketone bodies
Protein breakdown that supplies urea nitrogen
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: define nontemplate precisely
items.prompt: Which statement best defines nontemplate lipid synthesis?
options: Lipids assemble randomly without enzymes
Every lipid carbon is copied from messenger RNA
Enzymes build lipids without a sequence template
Lipids cannot be regulated because no template exists
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: apply the template distinction
items.prompt: Which process directly uses a messenger-RNA sequence to determine monomer order?
options: Protein synthesis at a ribosome
Glycogen synthesis in the cytosol
Fatty-acid synthesis from acetyl units
Triacylglycerol formation from glycerol and fatty acids
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Starting check: identify the amino-acid pool
items.prompt: Dietary protein is digested. Which product enters the body’s shared pool for protein synthesis or further metabolism?
options: Amino acids available for reuse or breakdown
Intact glycogen molecules copied from the meal
Ketone bodies containing peptide bonds
Fatty acids carrying amino nitrogen unchanged
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Guided practice: separate nitrogen and carbon
items.prompt: An amino acid is used as fuel rather than incorporated into protein. Which broad sequence is required?
options: Store the intact amino acid permanently in adipose droplets
Convert the amino group directly into glucose
Send the whole amino acid unchanged through beta oxidation
Separate nitrogen disposal from carbon metabolism
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Less help: identify nitrogen disposal
items.prompt: At bounded BIO depth, which product is the main endpoint for disposal of excess amino nitrogen in humans?
options: Glucose
Urea
Glycogen
Cholesterol
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: On your own: reject a dedicated protein store
items.prompt: Which statement best describes body protein in fuel metabolism?
options: A dedicated protein depot stores excess amino acids unchanged
Protein can never contribute carbon to energy metabolism
Functional proteins turn over; no separate fuel depot exists
All dietary amino acids are excreted without reuse
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Near exit: trace excess amino-acid use
items.prompt: Amino-acid intake exceeds immediate synthesis needs. Which fate is most consistent?
options: Store every intact amino acid in a permanent reserve
Convert all amino nitrogen into fatty acids
Send intact amino acids through glycogenesis
Dispose of nitrogen and metabolize the carbon skeleton
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Changed exit: predict fasting protein contribution
items.prompt: During prolonged fasting, muscle protein breakdown increases. Which liver process can some amino-acid carbon skeletons support?
options: Carbon can support glucose; nitrogen goes toward urea
Direct storage of intact amino acids as glycogen
Synthesis of DNA from whole protein molecules
Beta oxidation of intact peptide chains
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: use the two-destination model
items.prompt: When an amino acid is broken down, which pair of destinations must be tracked?
options: Nitrogen to disposal; carbon to central metabolism
Nitrogen toward glycogen and carbon toward messenger RNA
The whole amino acid toward beta oxidation and bile
Peptide bonds toward ketone storage and DNA
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: trace a new excess case
items.prompt: A hepatocyte oxidizes amino acids after synthesis needs are met. Which description is correct?
options: It stores all intact amino acids in glycogen granules
Handle nitrogen for disposal and metabolize carbon skeletons
It converts peptide bonds directly into ketone bodies
It sends intact amino acids through fatty-acid beta oxidation
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: bound the fasting claim
items.prompt: Which statement is appropriately bounded for protein use during prolonged fasting?
options: Every amino acid follows one identical advanced pathway
Protein becomes the only fuel in every tissue
Some amino-acid carbon skeletons can support glucose production
Amino nitrogen is converted directly into glucose carbon
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: apply the fasting branch
items.prompt: During fasting, an amino acid contributes its carbon skeleton to hepatic glucose production. What happens to its nitrogen at bounded depth?
options: It becomes part of the glucose molecule unchanged
It is stored permanently in glycogen
It enters fatty-acid beta oxidation as nitrogen gas
Nitrogen enters disposal pathways and ultimately urea
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Starting check: distinguish flux from pool size
items.prompt: A metabolite pool remains at 5 mmol while 2 mmol/min enters and 2 mmol/min leaves. Which statement is correct?
options: The pathway has zero flux because concentration is constant
Only the input reaction is active
Only the output reaction is active
Dynamic steady state with ongoing flux
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Guided practice: predict a high-energy response
items.prompt: A catabolic control enzyme is inhibited allosterically by high ATP. ATP rises sharply. What is the immediate predicted effect?
options: The enzyme is translated into a different protein
Flux through the controlled catabolic step decreases
Every pathway in the cell stops permanently
ATP crosses the nucleus and rewrites DNA
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Less help: locate peptide-hormone signaling
items.prompt: Insulin is a peptide hormone. What is its first bounded signaling location at a target cell?
options: A DNA sequence inside the nucleus
A mitochondrial beta-oxidation intermediate
A receptor at the cell surface
A glycogen branch point acting as a receptor
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: On your own: predict fed-state direction
items.prompt: After a meal, insulin signaling rises in liver and muscle. Which net direction is most consistent?
options: Greater glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis
Maximal glycogen breakdown and ketone export
Immediate proteolysis in every tissue
Permanent shutdown of all metabolic flux
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Near exit: analyze reciprocal pathway control
items.prompt: A fed-state signal activates glycogen synthesis and inhibits glycogen breakdown in the same tissue. What is the functional result?
options: Both opposing pathways run maximally at once
The glycogen pool must disappear immediately
The signal converts glycogen directly into protein
Net flux favors storage and limits futile cycling
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Changed exit: interpret a steady-state graph
items.prompt: A graph shows pool concentration constant while both synthesis and consumption rates rise from 1 to 3 units/min and remain equal. What changed?
options: The pool stopped all turnover
Flux rises while the pool remains at steady state
Synthesis ceased while consumption continued
The metabolite became a hormone receptor
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: apply the reciprocal-control rule
items.prompt: Why are opposing storage and mobilization pathways often regulated reciprocally?
options: To force both pathways to consume maximum energy together
To eliminate every enzyme from one pathway
To direct net flux and limit futile cycling
To make hormone structure irrelevant
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: predict a fasting direction
items.prompt: During fasting, glucagon signaling rises in liver. Which net direction is most consistent?
options: Greater hepatic glycogen breakdown and glucose support
Maximal glycogen synthesis from abundant dietary glucose
Direct glucagon diffusion to nuclear DNA
Permanent cessation of fatty-acid mobilization
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Repair: separate concentration and flux
items.prompt: A pool concentration is constant. What additional information is needed to decide whether flux is zero or high?
options: The color used to draw the pool
Whether the enzyme name is long
The number of peptide hormones in a catalog
The pool’s input and output rates
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: read a new rate table
items.prompt: A rate table shows 4 units/min entering a pool and 4 units/min leaving while concentration is unchanged. Which description fits?
options: The pool has no active reactions
Steady state with 4 units/min of flux
Only synthesis occurs at 8 units/min
Only consumption occurs at 8 units/min
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it to receive feedback.
